title: Hosting fallback & circuit-breaker brief: hosted → dedicated → private
body:
Executive summary:

This brief proposes a guarded, observable hosting strategy for customer POCs that need predictable latency and cost while retaining a low-friction path to dedicated or private deployments. The central idea: treat the hosted environment as the primary control-plane for onboarding, but implement a routing and circuit-breaker layer that enforces capacity-aware burst behavior and graceful fallback to dedicated/private variants. The document outlines topology options, traffic policies, safety gates, cost/latency tradeoffs, monitoring signals, and an operational runbook for solutions engineers during POC engagements.

Context and motivation:
- Customer POCs frequently begin on hosted (fastest time-to-value) but quickly run into throughput, data residency, or compliance limits.
- Full private/dedicated onboarding is often slow and expensive up-front; customers want a predictable, low-risk growth path.
- Without clear guardrails, sudden traffic spikes or model regresses cause outages or cost escalations that sour customer relationships.

Goals:
1) Provide a predictable, observable transition path from hosted → dedicated → private.
2) Ensure POC workloads stay within agreed cost and latency envelopes.
3) Automate safe burst behavior with circuit-breakers to avoid noisy-neighbor or model-level failure modes.
4) Make operational decisions reversible and visible to customer and SE.

Proposal overview (high-level):
- Control plane: Redwood-hosted control and orchestration during the POC period.
- Data plane: Primary serving in hosted mode; optional reserved capacity (Dedicated) for predictable throughput; Private (VPC/on-prem) for regulated customers.
- Router: Edge routing tier that can direct requests based on policy to hosted, dedicated, or private variants. Router also enforces circuit-breaker policies (rate, latency, error budget) and can trigger automated fallbacks.

Three candidate topologies (textual diagrams):
1) Single-router with staged variants (recommended for most POCs)
   - Edge Router -> Hosted model(s)
                 -> Dedicated pool (warm)
                 -> Private endpoint (configured)
   - Hosted is default. Router maintains per-tenant state and can shift percentages. A warm dedicated pool is provisioned only when committed or when traffic crosses a threshold.

2) Dual-router split (latency-sensitive customers)
   - Global Router -> Regional Router A -> Hosted/Dedicated
                 -> Regional Router B -> Private (VPC egress)
   - Used when data sovereignty/regional egress constraints exist; separate control for private paths.

3) Edge-first private preference (regulated customers)
   - Edge Router -> Private if available -> Dedicated -> Hosted as fallback
   - Private endpoints register health and capacity; only fall back to hosted under explicit policy.

Circuit-breaker and fallback semantics (core):
- Signals considered: 5xx error rate, p95 latency, queue depth, token-per-second consumption, KV cache hit rate, model quality alerts (eval regressions).
- Threshold examples (defaults):
  * error_rate > 1.5% over 5m -> trip breaker for 2m and failover to next variant.
  * p95 latency > 700ms for generation endpoints -> shift 30% traffic away until p95 < 500ms.
  * sustained RPS increase > 4x baseline for 1m -> throttle burst to 2x baseline and engage dedicated warm pool.
- Failure modes: if dedicated pool saturated and private not configured, router can enforce 429 or queue longest-wait requests, or apply degradation model (shorter max tokens, smaller beam width).

Burst and warm-pool policy:
- Warm-pool sizing heuristic: provision dedicated GPUs equal to 20% of sustained peak observed during a 24h window, adjustable by SLA.
- Burst to hosted: allow short bursts (<= 60s) above committed throughput at increased cost with explicit customer consent. Post-burst, recommend autoscale evaluation.
- Auto-warm triggers: high-confidence spike (RPS > 2.5x baseline for 3x consecutive 20s buckets) triggers a provisioning ticket and optional warm-pool spin-up.

Cost/latency tradeoffs:
- Hosted: fastest onboarding, variable cost, best for early functional validation. Latency depends on shared queues and backend model variants.
- Dedicated: higher predictable monthly cost, better tail latency, private instance isolation. Best when throughput and p95/p99 stability are required.
- Private: highest set-up friction, data residency, and network complexity; best for regulated/high-security workloads.
- SE recommendation pattern: start hosted with strict circuit-breaker defaults, measure 1–2 weeks, then propose dedicated only if jitter/costs exceed thresholds in our decision checklist (see later).

Monitoring, alerts, and SLOs:
- SLOs: p95 < X ms (depends on model family); error_rate < 1%; availability > 99.9% for dedicated customers.
- Dashboards: per-tenant token cost, token-per-second, p50/p95/p99 latencies, queue depth, dedicated pool utilization, fallback counts (hosted->dedicated).
- Alerts: initial pager thresholds for SE/ops: fallback_count > 3 in 10m; dedicated_utilization > 85% for 5m; sudden token cost > 2x forecast for a day.
- Observability hooks: capture request samples (scrubbed), prompt set quality checks, and model-side traces for debugging.

Operational runbook (SE-facing, step-by-step):
1) Onboarding (Day 0): enable tenant on hosted; configure router with default CB thresholds and billing consent for burst.
2) Baseline period (Days 0–7): collect traffic profile (RPS, tokens, latencies) and tag key endpoints.
3) Review (Day 7): run cost/latency heuristic; if p95 or cost consistently above target, propose dedicated warm-pool with estimated size and cost.
4) Warm-pool testing: shift 10% of traffic to dedicated for 10m; monitor errors and latency; increase gradually to 50% before full cutover.
5) Canary/private onramp: if private required, validate network egress (VPC peering), sign data-handling addendum, test with small request set, then sweep traffic with canary percentage increases.
6) Circuit-breaker event handling: if a CB trips, inform customer (automated email + SE Slack), open incident ticket, and follow triage steps: revert recent model changes, throttle requests, enable degraded mode (shorter generations), and spin dedicated if warranted.

Security & compliance notes:
- Private endpoints must register CA-signed certs and acceptable cipher suites; mutual TLS optional.
- Hosted logs/excerpts shared with SE must be scrubbed for PII before escalation.
- For data residency: router routing must respect region tags on customer; do not fall back across sovereignty boundaries unless explicitly allowed in contract.

Decision checklist (quick heuristic for recommending a move off hosted):
- Sustained token spend > $X/day for 14 consecutive days -> propose Dedicated.
- p95 latency deviation > 2x hosted baseline (and impacting user flows) -> propose Dedicated.
- Customer requires on-prem or VPC-only access -> propose Private.
- Model size / KV working set causes hosted tail spikes due to cold caches -> propose Dedicated with warmed KV caches.

Open questions and risks:
- Warm-pool cost modeling: how granular should warm-pools be per-tenant vs pooled across customers? (Cost efficiency vs isolation).
- SLA guarantees when traffic is split across hosted and dedicated: how to present a single availability number?
- Rollback semantics for model regressions that only appear on dedicated (due to different hardware kernels).

Customer communication templates (short):
- Pre-onboard: "We will start your POC on our hosted environment. If you need higher throughput, we can provision dedicated capacity. During spikes we have safeguards to protect you and our platform; we'll notify you before any cost-impacting burst beyond your agreed limits."
- On circuit-breaker event: "We've observed elevated error rates and temporarily routed your traffic to a safer capacity tier. Our SEs are investigating and will provide an update within 30 minutes."

Next steps and recommended SE actions:
- Pilot this guarded routing with 2–3 upcoming POCs (preferably customers with clear throughput variance).
- Create a small automation to auto-open JIRA tickets when warm-pool triggers occur and include SE on the ticket. (JIRA:SOL-1987 is seed).
- Iterate CB thresholds after 30 days of production data; publish recommended profiles per model-family.

Appendix — quick reference knobs (defaults we suggest can ship in the SE playbook):
- CB: error_rate_trip=1.5% (5m), cooldown=2m;
- Latency shift: p95_trip=700ms, shift_fraction=30%, reassess_window=5m;
- Burst policy: allow 2x baseline for 60s with explicit billing consent; automated escalation to SE if >3 bursts/day.

Notes to self / TODOs (rough):
- Add sample Nginx/Envoy routing config for the Edge Router.
- Run simulation for cost impact of 20% warm-pool across 10 customers.
- Draft customer-facing one-pager for "What happens when we fall back".

---
End of brief.

(Working draft — intended to be iterated after the pilot POC runs. Contact: maya.patel@redwood.example for questions.)
